patient.chief_complaint: Persistent confusion and inappropriate speech after brief shaking episode, not returning to baseline over 30 minutes
patient.hpi: A 42-year-old Asian female teacher was brought to the emergency department by her husband after a witnessed brief generalized convulsion at home. Her husband reports she had been complaining of a severe headache for three days and had been 'not herself' — forgetting words mid-sentence and seeming confused about the day of the week. She has no prior history of seizures or epilepsy. The shaking episode lasted approximately 2 minutes then stopped on its own, but she did not regain her normal level of consciousness. When EMS arrived 8 minutes after the seizure, she was awake but confused, answering questions with inappropriate words, and appeared agitated. In the ED she is minimally following commands, oriented only to her name. She has a history of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) diagnosed 6 years ago, currently in clinical remission per her rheumatologist. She takes hydroxychloroquine and a low-dose prednisone taper she started 10 days ago for mild joint flares. She also takes levetiracetam — her husband mentions she recently started this medication but cannot recall the dose. Her blood pressure at home has been elevated per recent records. No fevers, no sick contacts, no recent travel. No family history of epilepsy. Social history: non-smoker, no alcohol, no illicit drugs, married with two children, originally from South Korea, lives in the US for 12 years.

eeg.impression: ABNORMAL EEG. Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) from left temporal-occipital region. Continuous rhythmic delta with embedded sharp waves meeting Salzburg criteria for NCSE. LPDs between ictal runs indicate significant epileptiform burden. No prior EEG for comparison. Clinical correlation recommended.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial hemorrhage. Subtle bilateral posterior hypodensity — early PRES (posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome) pattern vs ictal edema. MRI with gadolinium urgently recommended. BP 172/108 at time of presentation; hypertensive emergency should be considered.
recommended_actions: Urgent MRI brain with FLAIR and DWI to evaluate for PRES
Blood pressure management — reduce gradually to target <160/100 over 6 hours
Do not over-aggressively lower BP (may worsen cerebral perfusion)

findings.location: bilateral parieto-occipital lobes, posterior frontal lobes

output.impression: Classic pattern of posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). Bilateral symmetric parieto-occipital FLAIR hyperintensity with no DWI restriction (ADC elevated = vasogenic edema). Additional left temporal FLAIR signal corresponds to NCSE focus. PRES precipitated by hypertensive emergency (BP 172/108) in the context of SLE and steroid use. PRES-associated NCSE is the unifying diagnosis. Clinical correlation recommended.

Significant improvement in NCSE with BP control and AED escalation. Residual LPDs (ictal-interictal continuum) but no sustained electrographic seizures. Continue monitoring. Clinical correlation recommended.

interactions.description: Hydroxychloroquine can lower seizure threshold — minor but relevant in context of SLE-related NCSE
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Do not discontinue hydroxychloroquine (withdrawal can worsen SLE flare); seizure management via AED and BP control

interactions.description: Prednisone may lower seizure threshold via multiple mechanisms including hyperglycemia, fluid shifts, and direct excitatory effects
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Once PRES/NCSE resolved and BP controlled, taper prednisone cautiously with rheumatology guidance

output.summary: No major pharmacokinetic interactions. Hydroxychloroquine and prednisone each have mild pro-convulsant potential but should be continued for SLE control. Prioritize BP control and AED escalation for PRES-associated NCSE.

results.title: PRES in systemic lupus erythematosus: clinical features and outcome
results.key_finding: PRES occurs in 0.4-1.9% of SLE patients. Hypertensive emergency is the most common precipitant. Seizures occur in >70% of SLE-PRES cases. Full radiologic resolution in >90% with BP control. Recurrence risk if BP poorly controlled long-term.

results.title: Non-convulsive status epilepticus in PRES: diagnosis and management
results.key_finding: PRES-associated NCSE responds to BP control + AED. EEG monitoring essential. DWI restriction in PRES is rare and predicts poor outcome; absence of DWI restriction (vasogenic edema only) = good prognosis.

output.summary: PRES-associated NCSE in SLE is a well-recognized syndrome. Key precipitants: hypertensive emergency, steroid-induced hypertension, SLE activity. Treatment: urgent BP control is paramount and may be more important than AED escalation alone. Full recovery expected with adequate management.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) secondary to posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) in the context of hypertensive emergency and active SLE with subtherapeutic levetiracetam

differential.key_features: SLE with elevated dsDNA and low complement indicates SLE activity; however, PRES imaging pattern (posterior, no DWI restriction) and hypertension better explain the imaging than CNS vasculitis
CSF HSV PCR negative; MRI shows posterior not temporal-frontoparietal predilection of HSV; no fever or prodrome consistent with viral encephalitis
Autoimmune antibody panel negative in serum and CSF; subacute onset but PRES imaging pattern clearly visible; no psychiatric prodrome characteristic of anti-NMDAR
BP 172/108 elevated but PRES-specific MRI pattern present, distinguishing from diffuse hypertensive encephalopathy without structural imaging correlate

Escalate levetiracetam: IV loading dose 1500 mg then increase maintenance to 1000 mg BID

critical_actions: Emergent EEG to diagnose NCSE — confusion after brief seizure requires EEG for diagnosis
Urgent BP control with IV antihypertensive — PRES treatment is primarily BP reduction
MRI brain with FLAIR and DWI to confirm PRES — CT insufficient for PRES diagnosis
Escalate levetiracetam from subtherapeutic 500 mg BID to 1000 mg BID with IV loading
Do NOT over-lower BP — gradual reduction 10-15% in first hour; aggressive lowering risks cerebral hypoperfusion
contraindicated_actions: Over-aggressively lowering blood pressure (e.g., sodium nitroprusside to rapid normalization) — risk cerebral hypoperfusion in PRES
Delaying MRI and relying solely on CT — CT is insensitive for PRES; MRI with FLAIR is diagnostic
Stopping hydroxychloroquine abruptly — would worsen SLE flare which is a contributing precipitant
High-dose immunosuppression for 'CNS lupus' without first ruling out PRES — PRES requires BP control first, not aggressive immunosuppression
key_reasoning_points: PRES in SLE is precipitated by hypertensive emergency (BP 172/108) + steroid use — classic scenario requires urgent MRI
NCSE complicating PRES responds to BP control + AED; BP control is the primary treatment
DWI negative (no restriction) in PRES = vasogenic edema = reversible; DWI positive = cytotoxic edema = poor prognosis
Subtherapeutic levetiracetam (8 mcg/mL on 500 mg BID) is a contributing but not primary cause — inadequate dose for 42yo woman with body weight 58 kg
Elevated dsDNA + low complement = SLE systemic activity, but PRES (not CNS lupus vasculitis) is the imaging diagnosis based on posterior distribution + no DWI restriction
Resident-level challenge: NCSE in SLE patient requires integrating PRES imaging, BP management, rheumatology, and AED optimization simultaneously

metadata.teaching_points: PRES-associated NCSE; SLE as PRES precipitant; BP control as primary treatment; DWI absence = vasogenic = reversible; subtherapeutic AED contributing factor
metadata.pitfalls: Treating as CNS lupus vasculitis with aggressive immunosuppression instead of BP control; missing subtherapeutic levetiracetam; over-aggressive BP lowering
metadata.clinical_pearl: PRES-associated NCSE: MRI FLAIR shows posterior predominant changes. DWI negative = vasogenic = reversible. BP control is the primary therapy, not just AED escalation.
